content: Insect sting allergy refers to the allergic reaction that occurs in an individual following the bite or sting of an insect. The insects that most commonly cause allergic reactions are categorized into two groups: stinging insects, such as wasps, bees, hornets, and ants, and biting insects, such as mosquitoes and ticks. Stinging insects inject venom into their victims, while biting insects typically introduce anticoagulants into the skin. In most cases, individuals with insect allergies experience a localized allergic reaction at the site of the sting or bite. This reaction is characterized by swelling, which results from the release of histamine and other chemicals from the tissues near the affected area. The swelling can often be alleviated by applying an antihistamine ointment and using an ice pack. This type of localized reaction is the most common response to bites from biting insects and is experienced by many individuals to varying degrees. In some cases, mosquito bites can lead to a condition known as Skeeter Syndrome, which is a collection of symptoms that occur after a bite. This syndrome may be mistaken for an infection, such as cellulitis, due to its appearance. In individuals who are anaphylactic, the allergic response is much more severe and progresses beyond the sting site to involve the entire body. This systemic reaction can escalate to anaphylaxis, a potentially life-threatening condition. Anaphylaxis requires immediate medical attention as it can result in severe complications or death. Venom immunotherapy is a well-established treatment in North America and Europe for individuals who experience systemic allergic reactions to insect stings. This therapy significantly reduces the severity of allergic responses in affected patients. Regarding the epidemiology of stinging insect reactions, the majority of individuals who are stung by insects experience only localized reactions. However, it is estimated that 5-10% of individuals will develop a generalized systemic reaction, which can range from hives to wheezing and, in severe cases, anaphylaxis. In the United States, approximately 40 people die each year from anaphylaxis caused by stinging insect allergies. Additionally, about 8% of children are affected by insect sting allergies.
